boundary_rationale: The book opens on its own dated superscription, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה ("Yahweh spoke to Moses") anchored to the wilderness of Sinai and the first day of the second month, which opens the census command; the roster of twelve tribal representatives that follows (vv.5-15) is bound to that command by its own introducing clause, "these are the names of the men who shall stand with you," and the whole span closes on its own colophon in v.16 naming them קְרוּאֵי הָעֵדָה ("those called of the congregation").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the twelve-name roster (vv.5-15) away from the census command as its own register, but the roster has no independent opening formula of its own -- it is syntactically the direct object of v.5's "these are the names" -- so severing it would cut a single command-plus-witness-list unit in half.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.1 “Yahweh spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai…on the first day of the second month…saying”

oshb:Num.1.16 אֵ֚לֶּה קריאי קְרוּאֵ֣י הָעֵדָ֔ה נְשִׂיאֵ֖י מַטּ֣וֹת אֲבוֹתָ֑ם רָאשֵׁ֛י אַלְפֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הֵֽם (“these were the called of the congregation, the princes of the tribes of their fathers; they were the heads of the thousands of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: Narration pivots from Yahweh's command to Moses and Aaron's compliance -- וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן ("Moses and Aaron took") -- an execution notice distinct in grammatical subject and mood from the imperative-laden command it fulfills, closed by the recurring compliance tag כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה ("as Yahweh commanded").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep vv.17-19 fused with the register above on the theory that assembling the named men and counting the people are one continuous administrative act; but the shift from Yahweh's second-person instruction to third-person narrated fulfillment is the same command/execution seam this book marks repeatedly elsewhere, and treating it as scenery rather than boundary would blur that recurring device.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.17 “Moses and Aaron took these men who are mentioned by name”
oshb:Num.1.19 כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: Each of the twelve tribal entries repeats one identical template -- lineage clause, family/fathers'-house phrase, age threshold, then the tally verb -- with only the tribe name and the resulting number changing; because no entry introduces a new legal or procedural element, this reads as one register closed by its own grand-total colophon in vv.44-46, and extended through v.47's Levite-exclusion clause, which functions as the census total's own qualifying exception rather than the opening of the next unit. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-003-1), the twelve per-tribe petuchot standing after each tribe's own tally (approximately 1:21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39, 41, 43 -- "(two-witness)") are recorded here as preserved, addressed counterevidence: a mark this strong and this regular is real corroboration for reading each tribe as its own sub-unit, but per the owner addendum petuchah alone cannot drive a boundary, and it does not outweigh the register's own content-identity test (no entry introduces a new legal or procedural element), the same test M8-Num-176 applies openly to a comparable case rather than passing over in silence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer reading would give each tribe its own decision the way the camp order in ch.2 gets one per standard, and the twelve petuchot recorded above are real, marked support for that finer reading -- but ch.2's four camps differ materially in composition and each closes on a distinguishing march-order clause, whereas here all twelve entries are the same sentence with two variables swapped, so the marks corroborate a boundary the content itself does not independently support. Separately, v.47 could stay with the following Levite instruction (its original placement) rather than this register, but v.48's own fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula marks the true onset of that instruction, and the divine-speech formula opens a decision at twenty-two of twenty-four comparable sites across Num.1-10.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.20 “The children of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, their generations…all who were able to go out to war:”
web:Num.1.21 “those who were counted of them, of the tribe of Reuben, were forty-six thousand five hundred”
oshb:Num.1.44 אֵ֣לֶּה הַפְּקֻדִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ פָּקַ֨ד מֹשֶׁ֤ה וְאַהֲרֹן֙ (“these are they who were counted, whom Moses and Aaron counted”)
oshb:Num.1.47 וְהַלְוִיִּם לְמַטֵּה אֲבֹתָם לֹא הָתְפָּקְדוּ בְּתוֹכָם (“but the Levites after the tribe of their fathers were not counted among them”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh speech formula, כִּי דִבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.48), pivots the chapter's topic from counting fighting men to appointing tabernacle-carriers, matching the corpus-wide pattern in which a divine-speech formula opens a decision at twenty-two of twenty-four comparable sites in Num.1-10; the Levite-exclusion note that previously opened this span (v.47) now closes the census register instead (M8-Num-003), leaving this decision's own onset at the genuine formula boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.47 could remain this decision's own opening exception clause, since it names the very group v.48-53 goes on to instruct; but v.47 is a vav-disjunctive note attachable either direction, and the corpus-pattern of divine-speech-formula onsets is too regular across this stretch of the book to treat this one site as the exception without a stated reason.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.48 “For Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Only the tribe of Levi you shall not count’”
oshb:Num.1.54 וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“thus the children of Israel did…so they did”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן ("Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron"), opens the chapter and states the governing principle for everything that follows -- each man by his own standard, at a set distance around the Tent of Meeting -- before any specific camp is named, functioning as the superscription for the whole four-camp system rather than part of any single camp's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the Judah-camp entry that immediately follows it, since nothing else intervenes; but v.2's instruction is stated in general terms that apply equally to all four standards, not specifically to Judah's position, so treating it as Judah's opening would misassign a rule that governs the system as a whole to one camp within it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.1 “Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying”

oshb:Num.2.2 אִ֣ישׁ עַל דִּגְל֤וֹ בְאֹתֹת֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֔ם יַחֲנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מִנֶּ֕גֶד סָבִ֥יב לְאֹֽהֶל מוֹעֵ֖ד יַחֲנֽוּ (“every man by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers’ houses; they shall encamp around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it”)

boundary_rationale: The east-side camp entry is marked off by its own orientation clause, וְהַחֹנִים קְֳֵמָה מִזְרָחָה ("those who encamp on the east, toward the sunrise"), names Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun under one standard, and closes on the sequence-marking clause רִאשֹׁנָה יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out first").
strongest_rejected_alternative: The four camps could be treated as one undivided register the way ch.1's census tally is, since each entry shares a broadly similar shape; but unlike ch.1's twelve identical tribe-formulas, each camp here names a different trio of tribes and closes on its own distinct march-position clause (first/second/third/last), a functional distinction the pure census tally never carries.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.3 “Those who encamp on the east side toward the sunrise shall be of the standard of the camp of Judah”
oshb:Num.2.9 רִאשֹׁנָה יִסָּעוּ (“they shall set out first”)

boundary_rationale: A parallel orientation clause, עַל הַצּ֣ד נֶגֶמלע קֶ ("on the south side"), reopens the register for a different trio of tribes -- Reuben, Simeon, Gad -- and closes on its own ordinal marker, וְשְׁנִּיִם יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out second"), matching the east camp's form while naming distinct people.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since the internal formula (prince name, division count, cumulative total) is identical to the Judah camp's, a reader could argue this is mere repetition undeserving of a fresh boundary; but the orientation clause and the ordinal close are themselves the text's own device for segmenting the four camps, and ignoring them to save a decision would understate a marker the chapter itself uses four times over.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.10 “On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben”
oshb:Num.2.16 וְשְׁנִּיִם יִסָּעוּ (“they shall set out second”)

boundary_rationale: This single verse interrupts the four-camp sequence to place the Tent of Meeting and the Levite camp in the middle of the march, marking a different participant class (Levites, not a tribal standard) and a different kind of statement (a structural rule about march order rather than a roster entry), sitting precisely at the chapter's midpoint between the second and third camps.
strongest_rejected_alternative: It would be simpler to append this verse to the Reuben-camp entry that precedes it, since nothing marks a new speech formula here; but its subject is the Levites' Tent-of-Meeting position, not Reuben's division, and folding it into either neighboring camp would misattribute a rule about the whole march's structure to one tribe's register entry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.17 “Then the Tent of Meeting shall set out, with the camp of the Levites in the middle of the camps”
oshb:Num.2.17 וְנָסַע אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵד מַחֲנֵה הַלְוִּיִם בְּתוּךְ הַמַּחֲנֹת (“the Tent of Meeting shall set out, the camp of the Levites, in the midst of the camps”)

boundary_rationale: The register resumes with a third orientation clause, דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם…יָמָּה ("the standard of the camp of Ephraim…on the west"), naming Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, and closes on the third ordinal, וּשְׁלִשִׁים יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out third").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might merge this with the preceding Levite-hinge verse into one "west side" unit, but the hinge concerns march order for the whole camp while this span is a self-contained tribal register with its own prince names and totals; conflating them would erase the participant-class distinction the hinge verse exists to mark.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.18 “On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim”
oshb:Num.2.24 כָּל הַפְּקֻדִים לְמַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם...וּשְׁלִשִׁים יִסָּעוּ (“all who were counted of the camp of Ephraim…they shall set out third”)

boundary_rationale: The fourth and final orientation clause, דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה דָן צָפֹנָה ("the standard of the camp of Dan, on the north"), completes the fourfold structure, naming Dan, Asher, and Naphtali, and closes on the distinguishing rear-guard clause לָאַחֲרֹנָה יִסְעוּ ("they shall set out last"), a different ordinal marker from the other three camps'.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given that all four camps share the same three-tribe-plus-total shape, a minimal-split reading would treat vv.3-31 as one continuous four-part list needing no internal decisions at all; but each camp's own orientation-and-ordinal frame is a real, repeated structural device the text uses to segment the march, and collapsing all four into one span would erase that device entirely.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.25 “On the north side shall be the standard of the camp of Dan”
oshb:Num.2.31 לָאַחֲרֹנָה יִסְעוּ לְדִגְלֵיהֶם (“they shall set out last by their standards”)

boundary_rationale: After the fourth camp, the text steps back from the tribe-by-tribe register to a whole-book grand total (matching ch.1's), a repeated note that the Levites were excluded, and the closing fulfillment tag, וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה ("the children of Israel did according to all that Yahweh commanded"), a summary register-close distinct in function from any single camp's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This closing note could be attached to the Dan-camp entry as its final clause, since nothing separates them typographically; but v.32's total covers all four camps together, not Dan's alone, and the compliance formula in v.34 answers the whole chapter's opening command in v.1-2, so it functions as the chapter's close rather than the fourth camp's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.34 “Thus the children of Israel did…so they encamped by their standards, and so they set out”
oshb:Num.2.32 אֵ֚לֶּה פְּקוּדֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“these are the numbered ones of the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: A genealogical superscription, וְאֵּלֶּה תוֹלְדֹת אַהֲרֹן ומֹשֶׁה ("now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses"), opens a new topic (the priestly line, not the tribal census) and this unit is closed by the Nadab/Abihu death notice, which explains why only Eleazar and Ithamar remain active in the priesthood -- a self-contained genealogical unit before the Levites are ever mentioned.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because "generations" formulas elsewhere in the Torah often open much larger units, one could extend this span through the whole Levite material in ch.3-4; but v.5's fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula immediately begins a new topic (the Levites given to Aaron) with its own imperative, so the toledot notice reads as a self-contained priestly-lineage preface rather than the header for everything that follows.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.1 “Now this is the history of the generations of Aaron and Moses”
oshb:Num.3.4 וַיְכַהֵן אֶלְעָזָר וְאִיתָמָר עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם (“Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests in the presence of Aaron their father”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר, opens the imperative to bring the tribe of Levi near and set it before Aaron, closed on the same capital-crime refrain used for the sanctuary throughout this book, וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת ("the stranger who comes near shall be put to death").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the next speech formula's firstborn-substitution rationale (vv.11-13) as one continuous "Levites for Aaron" instruction, since both concern the same broad arrangement; v.11 reopens on its own fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula and shifts from procedural assignment (Levites serve Aaron) to theological rationale (Levites replace firstborns), a real change of register the formula break marks.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.6 “Bring the tribe of Levi near, and set them before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him”
oshb:Num.3.10 וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת (“and the stranger who comes near shall be put to death”)

boundary_rationale: A second fresh וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר formula shifts the topic from procedural assignment to theological grounding -- the Levites stand in place of every Israelite firstborn spared in Egypt -- closed by the self-identifying refrain אֲנִי יְהוָה ("I am Yahweh").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might fold this rationale into the census command that follows (vv.14-16), since both address the Levites' special status; v.14, though, carries a fresh formula of its own and a wholly different action verb (count, not take), so keeping the rationale statement distinct from the counting instruction it grounds better reflects two speech acts rather than one continuous command.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.12 “I have taken the Levites…instead of all the firstborn”
oshb:Num.3.13 לִי יִהְיוּ אֲנִי יְהוָה (“they shall be mine; I am Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: A third fresh messenger formula opens a distinct imperative -- פְּקֹד אֶת בְּנֵי לֵוִי ("count the children of Levi") -- setting a month-old-and-upward threshold that contrasts sharply with the twenty-year war-census age in ch.1, and closes on Moses' compliance notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since both this span and the census-execution register that follows concern counting the Levites, one could merge them into a single command-plus-results unit; but the register (vv.17ff) opens with its own distinct genealogical formula naming Gershon, Kohath, and Merari rather than continuing the command's second-person imperative, so I keep the command separate from the roster it authorizes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.15 “Count the children of Levi by their fathers’ houses…every male from a month old and upward”
oshb:Num.3.16 וַיִּפְקֹד אֹתָם מֹשֶׁה עַל פִּּי יְהוָה (“Moses counted them according to Yahweh’s word”)

boundary_rationale: The three-clan skeleton -- Gershon, Kohath, Merari, each immediately followed by its own sub-family names -- opens the detailed Levite register proper, closed by its own summary clause, אֵּלֶּה הֵּם מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַלֵּוִי לְבֵית אֲבֹתָם ("these are the families of the Levites according to their fathers' houses").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This bare name list could be treated as an inseparable heading fused to the Gershonite entry that immediately follows, since it has no count or duty of its own; but its own closing colophon (v.20b) marks it as a complete three-clan skeleton in its own right, structurally parallel to how the twelve-prince roster in ch.1 closes before the tribal counts proper begin.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.17 “These were the sons of Levi by their names: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari”

oshb:Num.3.20 וּבְנֵ֧י מְרָרִ֛י לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖ם מַחְלִ֣י וּמוּשִׁ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֛ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הַלֵּוִ֖י לְבֵ֥ית אֲבֹתָֽם (“the sons of Merari by their families: Mahli and Mushi; these are the families of the Levites according to their fathers’ houses”)

boundary_rationale: The Gershonite entry has the same five-part shape that recurs for Kohath and Merari -- sub-family names, count, camp position, prince, and itemized duty -- opened by its own clause לְגֵּרְשׁוֹן מִשְׂפַּחת ("of Gershon was the family of") and closed on its own itemized-duty list, distinguishing it structurally from the Kohathite and Merarite entries that share its form but not its content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The three clan entries could be merged into one register the way I merged the twelve tribes of ch.1, since all three share one five-part template; but unlike ch.1's tribes, each clan here carries a materially different duty list (curtains and coverings for Gershon; ark and furniture for Kohath; frames and pillars for Merari), so the template's content, not just its names and numbers, changes clan to clan.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.21 “Of Gershon was the family of the Libnites, and the family of the Shimeites”

oshb:Num.3.25 וּמִשְׁמֶ֤רֶת בְּנֵֽי גֵרְשׁוֹן֙ בְּאֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֔ד הַמִּשְׁכָּ֖ן וְהָאֹ֑הֶל מִכְסֵ֕הוּ וּמָסַ֕ךְ פֶּ֖תַח אֹ֥הֶל מוֹעֵֽד (“the duty of the sons of Gershon in the Tent of Meeting shall be the tabernacle, the tent, its covering, the screen for the door of the Tent of Meeting”)

boundary_rationale: וְלִקְהָת ("and of Kohath") reopens the register for the second clan, whose duty list -- ark, table, lampstand, altars, sanctuary vessels -- is distinct enough in content and gravity that a special chief-of-princes, Eleazar himself, is named to oversee it, a detail none of the other two clans receives.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep Kohath fused to Gershon under a single "Levite duties" span, treating the whole three-clan run as one topic; but the fresh וְלִקְהָת opening and the unique addition of a supervising prince over Kohath alone mark this as a structurally and functionally separate entry, not a continuation of Gershon's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.31 “Their duty shall be the ark, the table, the lamp stand, the altars, the vessels of the sanctuary”

oshb:Num.3.27 וְלִקְהָ֗ת מִשְׁפַּ֤חַת הַֽעַמְרָמִי֙ וּמִשְׁפַּ֣חַת הַיִּצְהָרִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֨חַת֙ הַֽחֶבְרֹנִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֖חַת הָֽעָזִּיאֵלִ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֖ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הַקְּהָתִֽי (“of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, the family of the Izharites, the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites; these are the families of the Kohathites”)

boundary_rationale: לְמְרָרִי ("of Merari") opens the third and last clan entry, whose duty list -- the tabernacle's frames, bars, pillars, and sockets -- is the structural rather than sacred-furniture portion of the tabernacle, completing the three-clan set begun at v.21.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because Merari's entry closely mirrors Kohath's in grammatical shape, a reader could treat vv.27-37 as one undifferentiated "remaining two clans" span; but Merari's own opening formula and wholly distinct duty content (structural framework rather than sacred vessels) mark it as the register's third discrete entry, consistent with how Gershon and Kohath were each given their own span above.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.36 “The appointed duty of the sons of Merari shall be the tabernacle’s boards, its bars, its pillars”

oshb:Num.3.33 לִמְרָרִ֕י מִשְׁפַּ֨חַת֙ הַמַּחְלִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֖חַת הַמּוּשִׁ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֖ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת מְרָרִֽי (“of Merari was the family of the Mahlites and the family of the Mushites; these are the families of Merari”)

boundary_rationale: The register shifts from clan-by-clan entries to Moses and Aaron's own eastward camp position -- a distinct participant class from the three named clans -- and closes the whole Levite census with its grand total, כָּל פְּקוּדֵי הַלְויִּם ("all who were counted of the Levites"), a summary-total function distinct from any single clan's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the Merarite entry as its closing clause, since nothing else intervenes structurally; but Moses and Aaron's priestly-family camp position is not a fourth Levite clan, and v.39's total sums across all three clans just named, functioning as this register's colophon rather than Merari's.

oshb:Num.3.38 וְהַחֹנִ֣ים לִפְנֵ֣י הַמִּשְׁכָּ֡ן קֵ֣דְמָה לִפְנֵי֩ אֹֽהֶל מוֹעֵ֨ד מִזְרָ֜חָה מֹשֶׁ֣ה וְאַהֲרֹ֣ן וּבָנָ֗יו שֹֽׁמְרִים֙ מִשְׁמֶ֣רֶת הַמִּקְדָּ֔שׁ לְמִשְׁמֶ֖רֶת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְהַזָּ֥ר הַקָּרֵ֖ב יוּמָֽת (“those who encamp before the tabernacle eastward, in front of the Tent of Meeting toward the sunrise, shall be Moses, with Aaron and his sons, keeping the requirements of the sanctuary”)

On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-052-1), a setumah stands after 7:11 itself -- the very verse this respan moved the onset onto -- and is disclosed here as weak-class corroboration against the respan; it does not outweigh v.11's own complete divine-speech formula under this campaign's evidence weighting, so the onset stands. Within the register, the introducing clauses fall into four groups, not the three originally claimed and not one uniform template (corrected per RVOL-M8-Num-052-2): day 1 (v.12) opens וַיְהִי הַמַּקְרִיב...לְמַטֵּה יְהוּדָה; day 2 (v.18) opens with a different verb form, הִקְרִיב, and no לְמַטֵּה clause; days 3-10 (vv.24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66) share בַּיּוֹם plus a definite ordinal (הַשְּׁלִישִׁי through הָעֲשִׂירִי); and days 11-12 (vv.72, 78) switch to an indefinite cardinal construction, בְּיוֹם עַשְׁתֵּי עָשָׂר יוֹם and בְּיוֹם שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר יוֹם, dropping both the definite article and the ordinal form. What remains uniform across every day, without exception, is the item list itself, beginning קַעֲרַת כֶּסֶף אַחַת...: word-for-word identical at every one of the twelve occurrences checked (7:13, 19, 25, 31, 37, 43, 49, 55, 61, 67, 73, 79).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given the confirmed four-way progression in the introducing clauses, the setumah after v.11, and the twelve petuchot marking each day's entry, a reviewer could reasonably split this into twelve per-day decisions, or at minimum into the four sub-groups the introducing clauses actually fall into, to match the fine granularity used for ch.2's camps and ch.3's clans. I hold the register whole because the offering content -- not the introducing clause -- is what those two comparison cases actually vary: ch.2's camps differ in tribes and march role, ch.3's clans differ in duty inventory, but every one of these twelve entries offers the identical items in the identical amounts, verified word for word. The four-way introducing-clause progression, the setumah at v.11, and the twelve closing petuchot are all real counterevidence, recorded rather than omitted; they corroborate a finer split without, on their own, outweighing the register's uniform substance.

boundary_rationale: וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹתָם ("and these are their names") opens the twelve-tribe roster in the same one-name-per-tribe template used for the census witnesses in ch.1, closed by the register's own colophon and the notable renaming of Hoshea to Joshua.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Following the ch.1 census precedent, one might expect this roster split at every name; but exactly as with ch.1's assistant-princes list, each entry is the identical "of tribe X, name son-of-name" formula with no functional variation, so I keep it as one register rather than twelve near-duplicate decisions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.4 “Of the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur”
oshb:Num.13.16 וַיִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה לְהוֹשֵׁעַ בִּן נוּן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (“Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Joshua”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own direct-speech instructions to the twelve -- what to observe about the land's fertility, fortification, and inhabitants -- open with וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם ("and said to them") and close on the narrator's dating aside, the time of first-ripe grapes, before the spies actually depart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the roster above as Moses' continuing speech to the men just named; but the roster is narration about the spies ("these are their names"), while this span is Moses' own direct quoted instruction to them, a change of both grammatical person and content.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.18 “See the land, what it is; and the people who dwell therein…”
oshb:Num.13.20 וְהַיָּמִים יְמֵי בִּכּוּרֵי עֲנָבִים (“now the time was the time of the first-ripe grapes”)

boundary_rationale: Narration shifts to the spies' own itinerary and the Eshcol grape-cluster episode, closed by the forty-day return notice, מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם ("at the end of forty days"), a datestamp bridging into the report scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep the return-notice (v.25) fused with the report scene that follows, since it directly leads into their arrival; but v.26 opens with its own fresh narration ("they went and came to Moses") describing a distinct action -- reporting, not traveling -- so the journey-and-return notice stays with the journey it summarizes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.23 “They came to the valley of Eshcol, and cut down from there a branch with one cluster of grapes”
oshb:Num.13.25 וַיָּשֻׁבוּ מִתּוּר הָאָרֶץ מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם (“they returned from spying out the land at the end of forty days”)

boundary_rationale: The spies arrive and give their joint report -- fertile land, fortified cities, the Anakim, and the surrounding nations' locations -- a single collective speech closed before Caleb's dissenting voice interrupts it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because Caleb's counter-speech and the majority's contrary report both respond to this same report scene, one could treat vv.26-33 as one continuous "the spies speak" unit; but v.30 opens with Caleb specifically silencing the people, a distinct speaker and rhetorical move from the collective report that precedes it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.27 “Surely it flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit”
oshb:Num.13.29 עֲמָלֵק יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב (“Amalek dwells in the land of the South”)

boundary_rationale: Caleb's own dissenting voice, עָלֹה נַעֲלֶה ("let's go up at once"), opens a direct contest against the other spies' fear-driven counter-speech, which escalates into the grasshopper self-comparison that closes the chapter and sets up ch.14's rebellion.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Caleb's speech (v.30) could be split from the majority's rebuttal (vv.31-33) as two decisions, since they are formally two speeches; but they are directly contrastive responses to the very same report with no narrative gap, forming one debate scene rather than two independent speech acts.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.30 “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!”
oshb:Num.13.33 וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּחֲגָבִים (“we were in our own sight as grasshoppers”)

boundary_rationale: The whole congregation's wailing response opens ch.14, וַתִּשָּׂא כָּל הָעֵדָה וַיִּתְּנוּ אֶת קוֹלָם ("all the congregation lifted up their voice"), escalating into an open proposal to appoint a new leader and return to Egypt, a distinct collective-action beat from the report scene it responds to.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the direct continuation of ch.13's grasshopper report with no fresh boundary; but a genuine shift from the spies' own report speech to the congregation's own collective reaction and proposal marks a new participant class taking the narrative stage -- a change of speaking subject the text itself marks, independent of and not corroborated by the chapter number that happens to fall at the same point (chapter divisions carry no evidentiary weight under the owner addendum).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.2 “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt”
oshb:Num.14.4 נִתְּנָה רֹאשׁ וְנָשׁוּבָה מִצְרָיְמָה (“let’s choose a leader, and let’s return into Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the assembly, and Joshua and Caleb's counter-appeal closes on their own reassurance; the congregation's stoning threat and the glory notice, וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה נִרְאָה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד (v.10), now close this decision as the appeal scene's own resolution rather than opening the judgment speech (respanned per OL-M8-Num-094-1).
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.10 could open the following judgment decision, the original reading, since the stoning threat escalates directly into Yahweh's proposal; but v.10 closes on the same theophany-notice shape already honored as boundary-bearing at 16:19/16:20 elsewhere in this book, and 14:11 opens with its own complete, freshly-addressed quotative frame, the stronger and more consistent seam.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.7 “The land…is an exceedingly good land”
oshb:Num.14.10 וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה נִרְאָה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד אֶל כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“Yahweh’s glory appeared in the Tent of Meeting to all the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's own proposal now opens this decision directly, וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.11), a complete fresh quotative frame matching the identical theophany-then-speech-formula shape already honored at 16:19/16:20, MT 17:8/9, and 20:6/7 in this book (respanned per OL-M8-Num-094-1: 14:10 now belongs to the preceding decision, M8-Num-093).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The theophany notice (v.10) could stay attached here as this decision's own opening, the original reading, on the strength of its direct escalation into Yahweh's speech; but the anaphoric אֹתָם in v.10 has its antecedent (Joshua and Caleb) in the preceding scene, and applying the same theophany-notice-closes-the-scene convention honored at three comparable sites elsewhere in this book argues for the same reading here.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.11 “How long will this people despise me?”
web:Num.14.12 “I will strike them with the pestilence, and disinherit them”

boundary_rationale: Moses' own extended intercessory speech -- appealing to Yahweh's reputation among the nations and quoting the divine attribute formula, יְהוָה אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד ("Yahweh is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness") -- forms one continuous petition closed on his final plea for pardon.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the quoted attribute formula (v.18) into two speech-units, since it functions almost as an embedded citation; but Moses introduces it himself with כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתָּ ("as you have spoken") as part of his own single continuous argument, not as a separately marked insertion.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.18 “Yahweh is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness”
oshb:Num.14.19 סְלַח נָא לַעֲוֹן הָעָם הַזֶּה כְּגֹדֶל חַסְדֶּךָ (“please pardon the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of your loving kindness”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's own answering speech opens with סָלַחְתִּי כִּדְבָרֶךָ ("I have pardoned according to your word"), pivots into the oath that the generation of complainers will not see the land, carves out the Caleb exception, and closes with the practical instruction to turn back toward the Red Sea.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the pardon/oath seam (vv.20-23 versus 24-25) into a forgiveness unit and a Caleb-exception unit; but both remain part of Yahweh's one uninterrupted reply to Moses' intercession, with no fresh messenger formula marking an internal seam until v.26's turn to the forty-years sentence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.23 “Surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers”
oshb:Num.14.24 וְעַבְדִּי כָלֵב עֵקֶב הָיְתָה רוּחַ אַחֶרֶת עִמּוֹ (“my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee messenger formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן, opens the formal sentencing speech proper -- one year for each of the forty days spied -- distinct from the more conversational pardon-and-instruction that preceded it, closed on Yahweh's own self-attesting oath formula, אֲנִי יְהוָה דִּבַּרְתִּי ("I, Yahweh, have spoken").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the pardon-and-turn-back speech above as its continuation, since the topic (consequences for the generation) is the same; but the fresh messenger formula reopens the speech with a wholly new rhetorical register -- day-for-a-year sentencing rather than personal pardon -- marking a distinct pronouncement.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.34 “after the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year”
oshb:Num.14.35 אֲנִי יְהוָה דִּבַּרְתִּי אִם לֹא זֹאת אֶעֱשֶׂה (“I, Yahweh, have spoken; I will surely do this”)

boundary_rationale: Narration reports the immediate fate of the ten spies who brought the evil report -- dead by plague -- against Joshua and Caleb's survival, a short execution-of-judgment notice distinct from Yahweh's own sentencing speech and from the presumptuous-attack narrative that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged into the sentencing speech as its concluding proof; but it is third-person narrated fact (the spies actually died) rather than Yahweh's own first-person pronouncement, marking a shift from speech to narrated consequence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.37 “those men who brought up an evil report of the land, died by the plague before Yahweh”
oshb:Num.14.38 וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן וְכָלֵב בֶּן יְפֻנֶּה חָיוּ (“Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive”)

boundary_rationale: Moses reports the sentence to the people, whose mourning turns to a presumptuous attempt to attack the hill country against Moses' explicit warning, closing the chapter on their defeat at Hormah -- a self-contained scene of disobedience distinct from the sentencing and its immediate aftermath.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at Moses' warning (vv.39-43) versus the attack and defeat itself (vv.44-45); but the warning exists only to be immediately and explicitly disregarded ("but they presumed to go up"), forming one tight warn-and-disobey-and-fail sequence rather than two separable beats.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.44 “they presumed to go up to the top of the mountain”
oshb:Num.14.45 וַיַּכּוּם וַיַּכְּתוּם עַד הַחָרְמָה (“and struck them and beat them down even to Hormah”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens a law explicitly framed for future settlement, כִּי תָבֹאוּ אֶל אֶרֶץ מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם ("when you come into the land of your habitations"), tiering the meal-and-drink offering by animal (lamb, ram, bull), closed by the recurring one-law-for-native-and-stranger refrain that seals the whole supplement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The three animal tiers (lamb, ram, bull) could each get their own decision the way ch.1's offering-torah material is split by animal class elsewhere in the Torah; but here all three tiers share one uninterrupted grammatical structure with no fresh protasis or messenger formula between them, differing only in the measured quantities, so I read the whole graduated scale as one register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.2 “When you have come into the land of your habitations, which I give to you”
oshb:Num.15.16 תּוֹרָה אַחַת וּמִשְׁפָּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וְלַגֵּר (“one law and one ordinance shall be for you and for the stranger”)

boundary_rationale: A second fresh messenger formula opens a distinct topic -- the wave offering of the first dough baked from the land's grain -- unrelated to the animal-offering scale above, closed on its own perpetuity clause, לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם ("throughout your generations").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could merge this with the animal-offering supplement above as one general "land-entry offerings" unit, since both are triggered by the same "when you come into the land" framing; but this span opens its own fresh messenger formula and addresses a materially different offering (dough, not livestock), marking a distinct instruction.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.20 “Of the first of your dough you shall offer up a cake for a wave offering”
oshb:Num.15.21 מֵרֵאשִׁית עֲרִסֹתֵיכֶם תִּתְּנוּ לַיהוָה תְּרוּמָה לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם (“of the first of your dough, you shall give to Yahweh a wave offering throughout your generations”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְכִי תִשְׁגּוּ ("and when you err"), opens the communal unwitting-sin remedy, specifying the congregation's bull-and-goat offering pair, closed on the blanket forgiveness formula that covers both native and stranger.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the individual unwitting-sin case that follows (vv.27-29) as one "unwitting sin" topic; but v.27 opens its own fresh protasis (וְאִם נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת, "and if a single soul") specifically distinguishing an individual from the collective case just given, a real change of legal subject.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.24 “all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering…and one male goat for a sin offering”
oshb:Num.15.26 וְנִסְלַח לְכָל עֲדַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכָם (“all the congregation of the children of Israel shall be forgiven, as well as the stranger”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis narrows the case from the whole congregation to a single soul, prescribing a year-old female goat, closed by the same one-law-for-native-and-stranger refrain used to close the land-entry offering scale above, binding the two case-types under a shared closing formula while keeping their distinct protases separate.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep this fused with the high-handed-sin contrast that follows (vv.30-31), since both concern categories of sin; but v.30 opens with a new contrastive subject, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה ("but the soul who does anything with a high hand"), explicitly opposing this unwitting case rather than continuing it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.27 “If a person sins unwittingly, then he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering”
oshb:Num.15.29 תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם לָעֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁגָגָה (“you shall have one law for him who does anything unwittingly”)

boundary_rationale: A sharp contrastive clause, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה ("but the soul who does anything with a high hand"), opens the defiant-sin case as the deliberate foil to the two unwitting cases just given, closed on the emphatic cutting-off penalty, הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת ("shall surely be cut off").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This two-verse contrast could be folded into the individual unwitting-sin case as its closing exception clause; but its own opening וְ-contrast and total absence of any offering remedy (unlike the two cases before it) mark it as a distinct legal category, not a footnote to the preceding case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.30 “the soul who does anything with a high hand…blasphemes Yahweh”

oshb:Num.15.31 כִּ֤י דְבַר יְהוָה֙ בָּזָ֔ה וְאֶת מִצְוָת֖וֹ הֵפַ֑ר הִכָּרֵ֧ת תִּכָּרֵ֛ת הַנֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַהִ֖וא עֲוֺנָ֥ה בָֽהּ (“because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him”)

boundary_rationale: A concrete narrative case interrupts the legal material -- וַיִּהְיוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר וַיִּמְצְאוּ ("the children of Israel were in the wilderness, and they found") -- narrating a specific man caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath, distinct in genre (narrative, not casuistic law) from both the high-handed-sin statute before it and the tassels command after it, closed by his execution.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this as simply illustrating the high-handed-sin category just legislated, folding it into that span; but this is narrated as a specific historical incident with its own custody-and-ruling procedure (v.34's "it had not been declared what should be done to him"), not a generalized legal case, marking a genre shift from statute to narrative.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.32 “they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day”
oshb:Num.15.36 וַיִּרְגְּמוּ אֹתוֹ בָּאֲבָנִים וַיָּמֹת (“and stoned him to death with stones”)

boundary_rationale: A final fresh messenger formula opens the tassels/fringes command, closed on the double self-identification refrain, אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם ("I am Yahweh your God") repeated at the very close of the chapter, tying the memory-device command back to the Exodus itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuous with the Sabbath-breaker narrative as one "remembering the commandments" unit; but the fresh messenger formula and the wholesale shift from a specific narrated incident to a general, perpetual command mark this as its own distinct legal instruction closing the chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.39 “that you may see it, and remember all Yahweh’s commandments, and do them”
oshb:Num.15.41 אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם (“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: A new named coalition -- Korah, Dathan, Abiram, On, and two hundred fifty princes -- opens the rebellion narrative with their own priesthood-contesting grievance, רַב לָכֶם, addressed jointly to Moses and Aaron, closed before Moses' own reply opens the next decision (re-cut three ways per OL-M8-Num-107-1: the identical 'Moses said to Korah' formula recurs at 16:8 and 16:16, and only the second occurrence was originally treated as boundary-bearing).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole of 16:1-11 could stay as one decision reading Moses' response as a single continuous speech-turn narrowing from the coalition-wide censer proposal to the Levite-specific rebuke, the original reading; but the identical formula opening Moses' reply at both 16:8 and 16:16 was treated as a boundary only the second time, an inconsistency of method rather than a defensible literary unity, and the resulting eleven-verse span ran more than double the length of every neighboring decision in this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.3 “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy”
oshb:Num.16.3 רַב לָכֶם כִּי כָל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים וּבְתוֹכָם יְהוָה (“you take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' response to the coalition's grievance opens with narration of his own falling on his face, closed on his censer-test instruction to Korah's whole company, וּתְנוּ בָהֵן אֵשׁ וְשִׂימוּ עֲלֵיהֶן קְטֹרֶת לִפְנֵי יְהוָה מָחָר, before his second, Levite-specific reply opens the next decision at the recurring 'Moses said to Korah' formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This span could stay merged with the coalition's opening grievance (16:1-3) as one continuous scene, since Moses' fall and his censer instruction directly answer that grievance with no intervening scene change; but Moses' own action (falling, then instructing) is a distinct narrative beat from the coalition's own speech, and isolating it lets the recurring 'Moses said to Korah' formula at v.8 do the same boundary-marking work it already does at v.16.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.4 “When Moses heard it, he fell on his face”
oshb:Num.16.7 וְהָיָה הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר יְהוָה הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ רַב לָכֶם בְּנֵי לֵוִי (“the man whom Yahweh chooses, he shall be holy. You have gone too far, you sons of Levi!”)

boundary_rationale: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל קֹרַח (v.8) reopens Moses' speech, narrowing from the coalition-wide censer proposal to a rebuke addressed to the Levites specifically -- 'is it a small thing that the God of Israel has separated you...do you seek the priesthood also?' -- closed on the charge that the whole company has gathered against Yahweh himself. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-264-1), this decision's own boundary rests on the verbatim pair וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל קֹרַח at v.8 and v.16 alone, letter for letter identical at both occurrences; v.5, Moses' first reply, is not a third instance of that same formula. v.5 reads וַיְדַבֵּר אֶל קֹרַח וְאֶל כָּל עֲדָתוֹ לֵאמֹר -- a different verb (דבר, not אמר), no subject named in the verse at all, and an addressee scope covering the whole company rather than Korah alone. The real case for a boundary at v.8 is that v.5's frame is unmarked in exactly these ways and v.8's is not, a sharper and more accurate ground than the original claim that v.8 'recurs' a formula already used at v.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could stay merged with the censer-test instruction (16:4-7) as one continuous speech-turn by Moses with no scene break, the reading originally adopted for the whole 16:1-11 span; but the reopening at v.8 is marked in three independent ways at once -- verb (אמר vs דבר), named subject (מֹשֶׁה vs none), and narrowed addressee (קֹרַח alone vs קֹרַח וְכָל עֲדָתוֹ) -- while v.5 itself carries none of v.8's marking, so treating v.5 as already 'the same formula' (the original rationale's own overstatement) is corrected here rather than repeated.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.8 “Moses said to Korah, ‘Hear now, you sons of Levi!’”
oshb:Num.16.11 לָכֵן אַתָּה וְכָל עֲדָתְךָ הַנֹּעָדִים עַל יְהוָה (“therefore you and all your company have gathered together against Yahweh”)

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the eighth-day solemn assembly that follows as "the end of Booths"; but v.35 opens with a materially different occasion, עֲצֶרֶת ("a solemn assembly"), not simply "the eighth day of Booths" in the same register-formula terms, and its own bull count (one, not a further decrease to six) breaks the arithmetic pattern entirely, marking a real functional shift, not just another day of the same feast.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.29.32 “On the seventh day: seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without defect”
oshb:Num.29.32 וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי פָּרִים שִׁבְעָה אֵילִם שְׁנָיִם (“and on the seventh day, seven bulls, two rams”)

boundary_rationale: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי עֲצֶרֶת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם ("on the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly") opens a distinct closing occasion, its offering reset to a single bull rather than continuing the Booths week's decreasing sequence -- a genuine break in the register's own arithmetic pattern, closed on the same layered-addition formula used throughout the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given its adjacency to Booths, this could be folded into the day-seven entry as an appendix; but its own distinct designation, עֲצֶרֶת, and its offering total's departure from the decreasing-bull pattern (a reset to one bull, not six) mark this as its own separately registered occasion, not simply Booths's own eighth day counted onward.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.29.35 “On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall do no regular work”
oshb:Num.29.38 מִלְּבַד עֹלַת הַתָּמִיד וּמִנְחָתָהּ וְנִסְכָּהּ (“in addition to the continual burnt offering, its meal offering, and its drink offering”)

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַיהוָה בְּמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם ("these you shall offer to Yahweh in your set feasts") closes the entire offering-calendar complex spanning chs.28-29 with a single summary rubric distinguishing obligatory feast offerings from voluntary vows and freewill gifts, a genre shift from register entry to closing generalization.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the eighth-day solemn-assembly entry as its closing clause; but its own אֵלֶּה opening explicitly generalizes back across the whole calendar ("in your set feasts," not just the eighth day), the same colophon-generalizing move used to close other legal complexes throughout this book.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.29.39 “You shall offer these to Yahweh in your set feasts—in addition to your vows and your free will offerings”
oshb:Num.29.39 אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַיהוָה בְּמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם (“these you shall offer to Yahweh in your set feasts”)

boundary_rationale: A short third-person fulfillment notice, וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("Moses told the children of Israel according to all that Yahweh commanded"), closes WEB's chapter division; the Masoretic tradition instead counts this identical clause as its own opening verse of ch.30 (MT 30:1), a genuine versification divergence I follow WEB's own boundary for while flagging the MT's differing placement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Following the Masoretic chapter numbering, this verse could be read as opening the vow-law chapter rather than closing the offering calendar; but on review, MT's own petuchah placement in fact agrees with WEB's grouping here -- the paragraph unit itself is not divided differently between the two traditions, only the chapter NUMBER assigned to this verse differs (MT counts it as 30:1, WEB as 29:40). The divergence between traditions is therefore a numbering artifact, not an underlying disagreement about where the paragraph boundary falls, which removes the main source of the uncertainty this decision was originally graded low for; confidence raised to medium accordingly. The verse's own subject (the whole congregation, addressed collectively) and content (a general compliance report) still matches the offering calendar's own recurring closing-formula pattern better than it matches ch.30's addressee-specific opening ('the heads of the tribes') that follows.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.29.40 “Moses told the children of Israel according to all that Yahweh commanded Moses”
oshb:Num.30.1 וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (MT 30:1 = WEB 29:40)

boundary_rationale: A fresh addressee -- רָאשֵׁי הַמַּטּוֹת ("the heads of the tribes"), not the whole congregation -- opens the vow-law material with its own superscription, זֶה הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("this is the thing which Yahweh has commanded"), stating the general male-vow rule before the casuistic sub-cases begin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the unmarried-daughter's-vow case that follows (vv.3-5) as one continuous opening movement; but v.3 opens its own fresh protasis, וְאִשָּׁה כִּי תִדֹּר ("and if a woman vows"), narrowing from the general male rule just stated to the first of four distinct female-vow sub-cases.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.2 “When a man vows a vow to Yahweh…he shall not break his word”

oshb:Num.30.2 (MT 30:3 = WEB 30:2) אִ֚ישׁ כִּֽי יִדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר לַֽיהוָ֗ה א֣וֹ הִשָּׁ֤בַע שְׁבֻעָה֙ לֶאְסֹ֤ר אִסָּר֙ עַל נַפְשׁ֔וֹ לֹ֥א יַחֵ֖ל דְּבָר֑וֹ כְּכָל הַיֹּצֵ֥א מִפִּ֖יו יַעֲשֶֽׂה (“when a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis narrows the general rule to the first female sub-case, an unmarried daughter still in her father's household, whose vow stands unless her father voids it the very day he hears it, closed on the forgiveness clause specific to a voided vow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the betrothed/married woman's case that follows (vv.6-8) as one "female vow" topic; but v.6 opens its own fresh protasis specifically distinguishing a woman "who has a husband" from the unmarried daughter just addressed, a materially different life-stage and authority structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.5 “if her father forbids her in the day that he hears, none of her vows…shall stand”
oshb:Num.30.6 (MT 30:6 = WEB 30:5) וַיהוָה יִסְלַח לָהּ כִּי הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ (“Yahweh will forgive her, because her father has forbidden her”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ ("and if she marries a husband"), opens the second female sub-case -- a vow made before marriage now subject to the husband's ratification -- closed on the same day-of-hearing forbid-or-forgive logic applied to the husband's authority instead of the father's.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the unmarried daughter's case above given the shared underlying father-or-husband-authority logic; but its own distinct protasis marking a change of life-stage (from father's household to husband's) is the same kind of casuistic list-item marker that separated every other sub-case in this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.6 “If she has a husband, while her vows are on her”
oshb:Num.30.7 (MT 30:7 = WEB 30:6) וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ וּנְדָרֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ (“and if she has a husband, while her vows are on her”)

oshb:Num.30.9 (MT 30:9 = WEB 30:8) וְאִם בְּיוֹם שְׁמֹעַ אִישָׁהּ יָנִיא אוֹתָהּ וְהֵפֵר אֶת נִדְרָהּ...וַיהוָה יִסְלַח לָהּ (“and if her husband disallows her in the day that he hears it, then he makes void her vow…Yahweh will forgive her”)

boundary_rationale: A single-verse case addresses the widow or divorced woman specifically -- וְנֵדֶר אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה ("but the vow of a widow, or of her who is divorced") -- whose vow stands absolutely, with no male authority left to ratify or void it, the shortest and most legally distinct of the four female sub-cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given its brevity, this could be folded into either the preceding married-woman case or the following married-woman-in-her-husband's-house case; but its own protasis names a wholly distinct legal category (a woman under no man's authority at all) whose rule is the simple opposite of every other case in the chapter -- her vow always stands -- meriting its own decision despite its length.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.9 “But the vow of a widow, or of her who is divorced, everything…shall stand against her”
oshb:Num.30.10 (MT 30:10 = WEB 30:9) כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָסְרָה עַל נַפְשָׁהּ יָקוּם עָלֶיהָ (“everything with which she has bound her soul shall stand against her”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְאִם בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה ("and if she vowed in her husband's house"), opens the fourth and longest sub-case -- a woman already married when she vows -- closed on the delayed-objection ruling that a husband who waits past the day of hearing bears his wife's iniquity himself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the day-of-hearing/delayed-objection seam (vv.10-12 versus 13-15) as two decisions; but both halves address the same married-woman case under one continuous protasis with no fresh introductory formula between them, the delayed-objection ruling functioning as this case's own closing elaboration rather than a fresh sub-case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.13 “Every vow, and every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband may establish it, or her husband may make it void”
oshb:Num.30.16 (MT 30:16 = WEB 30:15) וְנָשָׂא אֶת עֲוֺנָהּ (“then he shall bear her iniquity”)

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים ("these are the statutes") closes the whole vow-law chapter with a generalizing colophon naming its three governing relationships -- husband-wife, father-daughter -- the same colophon-generalizing device used to close the sotah and Nazirite laws in chs.5-6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the married-woman case above as its closing clause; but its own אֵלֶּה opening explicitly restates the whole chapter's legal scope rather than continuing the specific married-woman case just concluded, the recognized colophon pattern I treat consistently across this book.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.16 “These are the statutes which Yahweh commanded Moses, between a man and his wife”
oshb:Num.30.17 (MT 30:17 = WEB 30:16) אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“these are the statutes which Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the Midianite war with its own vengeance rationale, נְקֹם נִקְמַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("avenge the children of Israel"), explicitly tied back to Balaam's own role in the Peor affair, closed on the levy's own precise count -- twelve thousand, one thousand per tribe -- before battle is joined.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the battle report (vv.7-12) as one continuous "the war" unit; but the levy's own completed count (v.5-6) is a distinct administrative milestone closed before any fighting is narrated, and v.7's fresh action verb, וַיִּצְבְּאוּ ("they made war"), opens the campaign proper as a separate beat.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.5 “So there were delivered, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from every tribe, twelve thousand armed for war”

oshb:Num.31.6 וַיִּשְׁלַח אֹתָם מֹשֶׁה אֶלֶף לַמַּטֶּה לַצָּבָא אֹתָם וְאֶת פִּינְחָס בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן לַצָּבָא וּכְלֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ וַחֲצֹצְרוֹת הַתְּרוּעָה בְּיָדוֹ (“Moses sent them, one thousand of every tribe, to the war with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest…with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand”)

boundary_rationale: וַיִּצְבְּאוּ עַל מִדְיָן ("they made war against Midian") opens the battle report itself -- every male killed, the five kings and Balaam himself among the dead -- closed on the plunder's arrival at the camp before Moses' own reaction is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Moses' anger at the surviving women (vv.13-18) as one continuous battle-and-aftermath unit; but v.13 opens with a fresh scene, Moses and Eleazar going out to meet the returning army, a distinct location and action from the battle and plunder-gathering just narrated on the field itself.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.8 “They also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword”
oshb:Num.31.12 אֶל הַמַּחֲנֶה אֶל עַרְבֹת מוֹאָב אֲשֶׁר עַל יַרְדֵּן יְרֵחוֹ (“to the camp at the plains of Moab, which are by the Jordan at Jericho”)

boundary_rationale: Moses and Eleazar's meeting of the returning army opens this movement, and Moses' own angry rebuke of the officers -- הַחִיִּיתֶם כָּל נְקֵבָה ("have you saved all the women alive?") -- closes on his explicit kill command for male children and non-virgin women, tying the command directly back to the Peor seduction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the meeting/rebuke seam (v.13 versus vv.14-18); but the meeting exists only to stage Moses' immediate angry question, with no independent content of its own apart from the rebuke it introduces, so I read it as one continuous confrontation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.15 “Have you saved all the women alive?”
oshb:Num.31.18 וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם (“but all the girls, who have not known man by lying with him, keep alive for yourselves”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own instruction shifts from the kill command to procedural purification -- seven days outside the camp, third-and-seventh-day rites for anyone who killed or touched the slain -- closed on the material-purification clause covering garments, skins, and wood.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the kill command above as its continuation; but it addresses a materially different concern (ritual purity of the victorious army, not the treatment of captives) using the same third-and-seventh-day timing already established for corpse contact in ch.19, marking a distinct procedural topic within the same speech.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.19 “Whoever has killed any person, and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves”
oshb:Num.31.20 וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂה עִזִּים וְכָל כְּלִי עֵץ תִּתְחַטָּאוּ (“all work of goats’ hair, and all things made of wood”)

boundary_rationale: A new speaker, Eleazar the priest rather than Moses, opens with his own colophon-style introduction, זֹאת חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("this is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded"), addressing the metals and fire-versus-water purification method, a distinct speaker and topic from Moses' own camp-purification instruction above.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the preceding purification span as its continuation, since both concern camp purity after battle; but the change of speaker (Eleazar, not Moses) and the shift from personal/textile purification to metal-object purification by fire mark a distinct instruction with its own colophon opening.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.21 “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded Moses”
oshb:Num.31.23 אַךְ בְּמֵי נִדָּה יִתְחַטָּא (“nevertheless it shall be purified with the water for impurity”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the plunder-division instruction, splitting spoil between the soldiers and the whole congregation, and prescribing distinct tribute rates for each half -- one in five hundred to Eleazar, one in fifty to the Levites -- closed on the Levites' own tabernacle-duty rationale.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the execution and totals that follow (vv.31-35) as one continuous division-and-accounting unit; but v.31 opens with third-person fulfillment narration, וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאֶלְעָזָר ("Moses and Eleazar did"), a distinct shift from the second-person instruction just given.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.28 “Levy a tribute to Yahweh of the men of war…one soul of five hundred”
oshb:Num.31.30 וְנָתַתָּה אֹתָם לַלְוִיִּם שֹׁמְרֵי מִשְׁמֶרֶת מִשְׁכַּן יְהוָה (“give them to the Levites, who perform the duty of Yahweh’s tabernacle”)

boundary_rationale: וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("Moses and Eleazar the priest did as Yahweh commanded Moses") opens the fulfillment notice, and the plunder's own grand totals -- sheep, cattle, donkeys, persons -- close this span before the half-by-half accounting begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the half-share accounting that follows (vv.36-47) as one continuous "the numbers" unit; but v.36 opens with its own fresh introducing clause, וַתְּהִי הַמֶּחֱצָה ("and the half was"), narrowing from the grand total just given to the soldiers' specific half-share breakdown, a distinct level of accounting detail.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.32 “the plunder…was six hundred seventy-five thousand sheep”
oshb:Num.31.35 וְנֶפֶשׁ אָדָם מִן הַנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר כָּל נֶפֶשׁ שְׁנַיִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁים אָלֶף (“thirty-two thousand persons in all, of the women who had not known man”)

boundary_rationale: וַתְּהִי הַמֶּחֱצָה ("and the half was") opens the detailed parallel accounting -- soldiers' half with its own tribute figures, then the congregation's half with its own tribute figures -- a register of twinned totals closed on the Levites' final receipt of the congregation's tribute.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into the soldiers'-half accounting (vv.36-41) and the congregation's-half accounting (vv.42-47) as two decisions, since each half is tallied separately; but both halves share one continuous parallel-structure register with no fresh messenger formula between them, and the second half is explicitly introduced as "of the children of Israel's half, which Moses divided" rather than as an independent new topic, reading as one twinned accounting unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.37 “Yahweh’s tribute of the sheep was six hundred seventy-five”

oshb:Num.31.47 וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָם לַלְוִיִּם שֹׁמְרֵי מִשְׁמֶרֶת מִשְׁכַּן יְהוָה כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“gave them to the Levites, who performed the duty of Yahweh’s tabernacle, as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A new movement opens as the army's own officers approach Moses voluntarily, distinct from the commanded tribute just accounted for -- their own gift of gold ornaments "to make atonement for our souls" -- closed on the memorial deposit of that gold in the Tent of Meeting, ending the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the half-shares accounting as its closing addendum; but this gold is explicitly distinguished as a voluntary gift the officers bring on their own initiative ("what every man found"), not the commanded one-in-fifty or one-in-five-hundred tribute just tallied, marking a materially different kind of offering with its own opening scene (the officers' approach) and closing purpose (memorial, not tribute).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.50 “We have brought Yahweh’s offering…to make atonement for our souls before Yahweh”
oshb:Num.31.54 וַיָּבִאוּ אֹתוֹ אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד זִכָּרוֹן לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (“brought it into the Tent of Meeting for a memorial for the children of Israel before Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: A new topic and new participants open ch.32 -- Reuben and Gad's great livestock holdings and their sight of Jazer and Gilead's grazing land -- closed on their own explicit request not to be brought across the Jordan, before Moses' rebuke begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through Moses' rebuke (vv.6-15) as one continuous request-and-response scene; but v.6 opens with Moses' own fresh speech, הַאַחֵיכֶם יָבֹאוּ לַמִּלְחָמָה וְאַתֶּם תֵּשְׁבוּ פֹה ("shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?"), a distinct speaking turn responding to the request just made. A closer alternative, considered and rejected: v.5 itself sits beside a setumah after v.4, and v.5 opens a second, resumptive וַיֹּאמְרוּ from the same petitioning speakers rather than a genuine addressee change; I judge the speaker change at v.6 (petitioners to Moses) the stronger, text-driven boundary, since it marks an actual change of speaking party rather than a same-party continuation of the request already begun.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.5 “Don’t bring us over the Jordan”
oshb:Num.32.4 אֶרֶץ מִקְנֶה הִוא וְלַעֲבָדֶיךָ מִקְנֶה (“it is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own extended rebuke opens with a rhetorical accusation, closed on the direct charge that this generation is rising up "in your fathers' place" to repeat the spies' own faithless discouragement of ch.13-14, explicitly recalling that earlier rebellion by name and consequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the historical-recollection seam (vv.6-9 versus 10-15), since vv.8-9 retell the spy narrative while vv.10-15 apply it as present warning; but Moses delivers both as one uninterrupted speech with no formula break, the recollection functioning as evidence within his single argument rather than a separate speech act.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.15 “if you turn away from after him, he will yet again leave them in the wilderness”

oshb:Num.32.15 כִּי תְשׁוּבֻן מֵאַחֲרָיו וְיָסַף עוֹד לְהַנִּיחוֹ בַּמִּדְבָּר וְשִׁחַתֶּם לְכָל הָעָם הַזֶּה (“if you turn away from after him, he will yet again leave them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all these people”)

boundary_rationale: Reuben and Gad's own answering proposal, גִּדְרֹת צֹאן נִבְנֶה לְמִקְנֵנוּ ("we will build sheepfolds here for our livestock"), opens their counter-offer -- build first, then fight alongside Israel -- closed on their explicit renunciation of any Cisjordan inheritance.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Moses' conditional acceptance that follows (vv.20-24) as one continuous negotiation; but v.20 opens with Moses' own fresh reply, אִם תַּעֲשׂוּן אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה ("if you will do this thing"), a distinct speaking turn responding to the proposal just offered.

oshb:Num.32.19 כִּי בָאָה נַחֲלָתֵנוּ אֵלֵינוּ מֵעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן מִזְרָחָה (“because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan eastward”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own conditional response, אִם תַּעֲשׂוּן אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה ("if you will do this thing"), opens the acceptance with its own positive and negative branches -- fulfillment brings the land, failure brings sin -- closed on his instruction to build the promised cities and folds regardless of the outcome.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the positive/negative-consequence seam (vv.20-22 versus 23-24); but both branches are stated as two sides of the same single conditional pronouncement with no fresh formula between them, reading as one continuous if/then-else ruling.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.22 “and the land is subdued before Yahweh; then afterward you shall return”
oshb:Num.32.24 בְּנוּ לָכֶם עָרִים לְטַפְּכֶם וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַאֲכֶם (“build cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep”)

boundary_rationale: Reuben and Gad's own short confirmation, עֲבָדֶיךָ יַעֲשׂוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר אֲדֹנִי מְצַוֶּה ("your servants will do as my lord commands"), closes the negotiation cycle before Moses' formal commission to the officials begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into Moses' conditional acceptance as its narrated response; but it is the tribes' own distinct speech act, a formal acceptance of terms rather than a continuation of Moses' own pronouncement, and it is followed by an administrative commissioning scene rather than more negotiation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.25 “Your servants will do as my lord commands”
oshb:Num.32.27 וַעֲבָדֶיךָ יַעַבְרוּ כָּל חֲלוּץ צָבָא לִפְנֵי יְהוָה לַמִּלְחָמָה (“your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: Moses formally commissions Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads, his continuing speech running from the commission itself (v.28) through his two-branch conditional charge (v.29-30) -- v.29 opens וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֲלֵהֶם, the identical 'said to them' construction already used at v.20, unmarked here as a continuation of the same speech act -- closing this decision before the tribes' own answer opens the next. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-232-1), the original ground for this split is corrected: it is not bare formula-recurrence across 'every other speaking turn' in the negotiation (32:16 in fact opens on a bare plural verb with no subject named at all, וַיִּגְּשׁוּ אֵלָיו וַיֹּאמְרוּ, and v.29's own formula matches v.20's exactly yet stays unit-internal here), but a change in verb TYPE at 32:31: וַיַּעֲנוּ בְּנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן ('they ANSWERED'), the negotiation's only response-form verb, marking the tribes' formal ratification of terms Moses has just set -- a different legal act in kind, not merely a fresh speaking turn like the ones that precede it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The commissioning and the tribes' answering oath could stay bundled as one legal transaction -- name witnesses, then ratify before them; that witnessed-oath reading has real force, and it is not defeated by treating every speaking turn in this negotiation as equally boundary-bearing, since it is not: 32:29's own 'Moses said to them' formula, identical to 32:20's, remains inside this span without being read as a fresh decision, so bare formula-recurrence cannot be the actual criterion. The split instead rests on 32:31's own וַיַּעֲנוּ marking a distinct act of ratification, unlike ordinary speech turns -- contrast the Edom negotiation (20:18, 20:20), where both of Edom's replies are plain וַיֹּאמֶר repeating the identical flat refusal with nothing new ratified, correctly kept as one continuous exchange (M8-Num-136) rather than split. The same verb-type distinction that merges Edom's exchange is what splits this one.

web:Num.32.30 “if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan”
oshb:Num.32.29 וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֲלֵהֶם (“Moses said to them” — identical to 32:20’s formula, unit-internal here)

oshb:Num.32.31 וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר (“the children of Gad and the children of Reuben answered, saying” — the negotiation’s only response-form verb, opening the following decision)

boundary_rationale: וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר opens the tribes' own formal, binding answer to Moses' commission, closed on their own restatement of the inheritance terms already agreed. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-266-1), the boundary is re-grounded on the verb type of וַיַּעֲנוּ ('answered') itself, the negotiation's only response-form verb, rather than on formula-recurrence generally: every earlier turn in this negotiation (32:6, 32:16, 32:20, 32:25, 32:29) uses ordinary speech-introducing verbs (אמר or a bare verb with no subject at all at 32:16), while 32:31 alone marks a distinct act of ratifying terms just set, not merely speaking.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could stay bundled with Moses' commissioning speech as one 'witnessed-oath' legal transaction -- naming witnesses, then ratifying before them; the original defense of the split (that 'every other turn' in this negotiation is bounded by the same named-speaker formula) overstated the pattern, since 32:16 names no speaker at all and 32:29 repeats 32:20's formula without triggering a boundary. The split holds on sharper ground: contrast the Edom negotiation (20:18, 20:20), where both replies are plain וַיֹּאמֶר repeating the identical flat refusal with nothing new ratified -- correctly merged as one continuous exchange (M8-Num-136) inside one bounded Masoretic paragraph (setumah 20:13, petuchah 20:21). Here, by contrast, ch.32 runs unbroken from the petuchah at 32:19 to 32:42 with no comparable external corroboration, so the split rests entirely on 32:31's own verb, marking the tribes' binding ratification as a different legal act in kind from Edom's repeated refusal-refrain -- a distinction in what is done with speech, not merely that speech occurs.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.31 “As Yahweh has said to your servants, so will we do”

oshb:Num.32.31 וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר אֵת אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל עֲבָדֶיךָ כֵּן נַעֲשֶׂה (“the children of Gad and the children of Reuben answered, saying, ‘As Yahweh has said to your servants, so will we do’”)
oshb:Num.20.18 וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו אֱדוֹם לֹא תַעֲבֹר בִּי (“Edom said to him, ‘you shall not pass through me’” — contrast: repeated plain refusal, no ratification, kept merged at M8-Num-136)

boundary_rationale: וַיִּתֵּן לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה ("Moses gave to them") opens the formal land grant to Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh, and the register of cities each tribe built and renamed closes this span before the Machir/Jair/Nobah clan-level notices begin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the Machir/Jair/Nobah conquests (vv.39-42) as one continuous "settlement" unit; but those notices concern individual clan leaders acting on their own initiative ("the children of Machir…went to Gilead, took it") rather than Moses' own formal grant and the tribes' own city-building already reported, a shift from official allotment to ad hoc clan conquest.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.33 “Moses gave to them…the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan”
oshb:Num.32.38 וַיִּקְרְאוּ בְשֵׁמֹת אֶת שְׁמוֹת הֶעָרִים אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ (“they gave other names to the cities which they built”)

boundary_rationale: Machir's own clan-level conquest of Gilead opens this decision, its plural subject and distinct verb sequence (וַיֵּלְכוּ...וַיִּלְכְּדֻהָ וַיּוֹרֶשׁ) unlike the Jair/Nobah naming template; it closes on Moses' own formal grant, וַיִּתֵּן מֹשֶׁה אֶת הַגִּלְעָד לְמָכִיר (v.40), the identical verb-plus-subject construction M8-Num-233 uses to define official Mosaic allotment (split per OL-M8-Num-234-1: the uniformity claim originally used to justify keeping all four verses together is false for 32:39, and v.40's grant language belongs with the official-allotment class, not the two ad hoc naming notices that follow).
strongest_rejected_alternative: All four verses (32:39-42) could stay one decision on the theory that all three notices share one template, the original reading; but only 32:41 and 32:42 actually share the personal-name-plus-הָלַךְ-וַיִּלְכֹּד-plus-naming template, while 32:39 has neither a singular named subject nor a naming clause, and 32:40's grant construction duplicates the criterion that defines the preceding span's own boundary, contradicting the uniformity claim this span was built on.

web:Num.32.40 “Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh; and he lived therein”

boundary_rationale: Two matched clan-level notices close the chapter, each sharing the identical personal-name-plus-הָלַךְ-וַיִּלְכֹּד-plus-naming template: Jair's own villages renamed Havvoth Jair, and Nobah's Kenath renamed after his own name, distinct in construction from Machir's own conquest-and-grant notice that precedes them.
strongest_rejected_alternative: These two verses could stay merged with Machir's conquest and Moses' grant (32:39-40) as one undifferentiated closing register, the reading originally adopted for all four verses; but Machir's plural subject and Moses' own grant-verb construction (וַיִּתֵּן מֹשֶׁה, duplicating the criterion that defines the preceding span's own official-allotment boundary) are genuinely distinct from Jair's and Nobah's shared ad hoc naming template, and treating all four as one template was the inaccuracy the challenge identified.
