boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("these are the journeys of the children of Israel") opens the itinerary catalog with its own explicit authorship note -- Moses wrote the starting points by Yahweh's own command -- a superscription distinct in form from every travel notice that follows it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the departure notice that follows (vv.3-4) as one continuous opening; but its own self-referential authorship claim ("Moses wrote…these are their journeys according to their starting points") functions as a title for the whole register rather than the register's first entry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.2 “Moses wrote the starting points of their journeys by the commandment of Yahweh”
oshb:Num.33.1 אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם לְצִבְאֹתָם (“these are the journeys of the children of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: A dated narrative aside opens the register's first substantive content -- the fifteenth of the first month, the day after Passover, Egypt burying its firstborn while Yahweh executes judgment on its gods -- distinct from the bare ויסעו/ויחנו formula that structures every station notice from v.5 onward.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded directly into the station-by-station register that follows as its first entry; but its content is narrative commentary (Egyptian mourning, divine judgment on Egyptian gods) rather than the bare travel formula every subsequent entry uses, marking it as the register's own narrative frame rather than its first station.

oshb:Num.33.4 וּבֵאלֹהֵיהֶם עָשָׂה יְהוָה שְׁפָטִים (“Yahweh also executed judgments on their gods”)

boundary_rationale: The register proper opens with the recurring formula וַיִּסְעוּ מִ...וַיַּחֲנוּ בְּ... ("they traveled from…and encamped at…"), repeated for every station from Rameses through Mount Hor with no narrative interruption; I read this whole thirty-three-verse run as one register rather than atomizing it per station, since each entry shares the identical two-verb formula and none introduces a new principle, only a new place name.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The task's own guidance warns against atomizing this catalog per station, but the opposite error -- reading all fifty-two verses of the whole itinerary (5-49) as one undivided register straight through Aaron's death -- would erase a real interruption; I split at v.37/38 specifically because the pure travel formula genuinely breaks there for a dated narrative aside (Aaron's death), then resumes unchanged afterward, so this first run ends where the formula itself stops, not at an arbitrary verse count.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.5 “The children of Israel traveled from Rameses, and encamped in Succoth”
oshb:Num.33.37 וַיִּסְעוּ מִקָּדֵשׁ וַיַּחֲנוּ בְּהֹר הָהָר בִּקְצֵה אֶרֶץ אֱדוֹם (“they traveled from Kadesh, and encamped in Mount Hor, in the edge of the land of Edom”)

boundary_rationale: The span 33:38-40 crosses the sole Masoretic paragraph mark reported in this stretch of the itinerary (a setumah after 33:39, per OL-M8-Num-238-1), binding Aaron's death notice to the Arad-king flashback as one interruption of the pure travel-formula register. 33:38 opens with וַיַּעַל אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן, a genuine motion verb ('went up') -- correcting the original claim that these verses 'contain no travel verb at all,' which was inexact -- though it is not the register's own recurring וַיִּסְעוּ/וַיַּחֲנוּ pair. 33:39 is a verbless summary closing the age-and-death notice, and 33:40 opens a fresh wayyiqtol with an entirely unrelated subject (the king of Arad), a real, checkable alternative seam independent of the setumah.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A seam at 33:39/33:40 -- splitting the Aaron notice itself from the Arad flashback -- is a genuine, text-supported alternative I tested and did not adopt: both verses share the same function of interrupting the travel-formula register with non-register content anchored at Mount Hor, and I read them as one coherent interruption unit rather than two further fragments, even though the setumah after 33:39 and the verbless-clause/new-subject shift both count as real, weighable evidence for the finer split. Per the instruction not to atomize this catalog, I hold the three verses together as the honest middle reading between treating the register as unbroken and cutting it at every available seam.

oshb:Num.33.40 וַיִּשְׁמַע הַכְּנַעֲנִי מֶלֶךְ עֲרָד…בְּבֹא בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“the Canaanite king of Arad…heard of the coming of the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: The pure travel formula resumes unchanged, וַיִּסְעוּ מֵהֹר הָהָר ("they traveled from Mount Hor"), continuing the register from where the Aaron interruption paused it, through to the final encampment in the plains of Moab -- the staging ground for the rest of the book -- again kept as one unsplit register consistent with the non-atomization reading applied to the first run.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could split this second run at any of its individual stations, matching a per-station reading someone might apply to the whole chapter; I reject that here for the same reason as the first run -- every entry is the identical two-verb formula with only the place name changing, and the chapter's own explicit instruction is to judge its internal structure honestly rather than atomize by station.

oshb:Num.33.49 בְּעַרְבֹת מוֹאָב (“in the plains of Moab”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens a wholly distinct genre -- command, not itinerary -- instructing the conquest of Canaan, destruction of idols, and division of the land by lot, closed on the warning that failure to drive out the inhabitants will leave them as thorns and pricks.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the itinerary register's own natural conclusion, since it follows immediately upon arrival in the plains of Moab; but the fresh messenger formula and the total shift from travel-notice form to imperative legal command mark a clean genre break, not a continuation of the ויסעו/ויחנו register.

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the land-boundary description with its own southern-quarter clause, וְהָיָה לָכֶם פְּאַת נֶגֶב ("and your south quarter shall be"), tracing the border from the wilderness of Zin to Azmon and the brook of Egypt, closed on that border's own terminus at the sea.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the western border (v.6) as one continuous circuit; but v.6 opens its own fresh clause, וּגְבוּל יָם ("and for the western border"), a distinct compass-direction heading matching the pattern each subsequent side of the border uses to open its own description.

oshb:Num.34.5 וְהָיוּ תוֹצְאֹתָיו הַיָּמָּה (“and it shall end at the sea”)

boundary_rationale: וּגְבוּל יָם ("and for the western border") opens the shortest of the four border descriptions -- the Mediterranean coastline itself serves as the boundary, needing no further tracing -- closed within the same verse on its own naming formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given its extreme brevity, this could be folded into either the southern border above or the northern border that follows; but its own fresh compass-direction opening clause is the same recurring formula marking every side of this border tour, and a one-verse entry is still a complete entry by that formula's own criterion.

oshb:Num.34.6 זֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל יָם (“this shall be your west border”)

boundary_rationale: וְזֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל צָפוֹן ("and this shall be your north border") opens the third leg of the boundary tour, tracing from the great sea through Mount Hor to Hazar Enan, closed on its own naming formula matching the western border's close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the western border into one "west and north" span, since both are relatively short; but each carries its own fresh compass-heading clause and its own distinct list of way-points, the same criterion separating every other side of this border description.

oshb:Num.34.9 זֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל צָפוֹן (“this shall be your north border”)

boundary_rationale: וְהִתְאַוִּיתֶם לָכֶם לִגְבוּל קֵדְמָה ("and you shall mark out your east border") opens the fourth and final leg, tracing from Hazar Enan down to the Jordan and the Salt Sea, closed on the whole boundary-tour's own summary colophon, זֹאת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם הָאָרֶץ ("this shall be your land").
strongest_rejected_alternative: The closing colophon (v.12b) could be split off as its own decision, matching how other זֹאת colophons were treated elsewhere in this book; but here it is a single short clause immediately capping the fourth border's own description with no independent content, so I keep it bound to the eastern border it closes rather than elevating it to its own span.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.12 “The border shall go down to the Jordan, and end at the Salt Sea”
oshb:Num.34.12 זֹאת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם הָאָרֶץ לִגְבֻלֹתֶיהָ סָבִיב (“this shall be your land according to its borders around it”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own instruction, זֹאת הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר תִּתְנַחֲלוּ ("this is the land which you shall inherit"), pivots from Yahweh's border description to Moses' own reminder that nine and a half tribes receive this land while two and a half already hold their portion east of the Jordan.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the eastern-border description as its practical conclusion; but it opens with its own fresh speaker (Moses commanding the people directly, not Yahweh speaking to Moses) and shifts from geographic boundary-tracing to administrative distribution logic, a distinct instruction.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.14 “the tribe of the children of Reuben…the tribe of the children of Gad…and the half-tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance”

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the naming of the land-division commissioners -- Eleazar, Joshua, and one prince per tribe -- in the same one-name-per-tribe template used for the census witnesses of ch.1 and the spies of ch.13, closed on its own colophon identifying these as the men Yahweh commanded for the task.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Following the census-witness precedent, this twelve-name roster could be split at every entry; but as with those two earlier registers, every entry here shares the identical "of the tribe of X, name son of name" formula with no functional variation, so I keep the whole roster as one register rather than twelve near-duplicate decisions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.18 “You shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land for inheritance”
oshb:Num.34.29 אֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה לְנַחֵל אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן (“these are they whom Yahweh commanded to divide the inheritance to the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the Levitical-cities instruction, צַו אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנָתְנוּ לַלְוִיִּם ("command the children of Israel to give to the Levites") -- the Levites' own promised compensation for holding no tribal land, per ch.18 -- closed on the general rule that the cities are for dwelling, the pasture lands for livestock.
